'''Bekku Ōyamazumi Shrine''' (別宮大山祇神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in '''Imabari, Ehime Prefecture'''. It is a '''Bekku (別宮, "secondary shrine")''' of {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|qid=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine|1=Ōyamazumi Shrine}}, the '''Ichinomiya (highest-Ranked shrine) of Iyo Province'''. It was formerly classified as a '''Prefectural Shrine (県社)''' and serves as '''Site 40 of the Shin Shikoku Mandala Pilgrimage (新四国曼荼羅霊場).'''  
== Overview ==  
[[File:別宮大山祇神社 鳥居.JPG|200px|thumb|Torii Gate]]  
Bekku Ōyamazumi Shrine is situated in central '''Imabari''', facing '''National Route 317'''. It is the Bekku (secondary shrine) of the '''Great Shrine of Japan’s Protector deity (日本総鎮守)''', {{ill|Ōyamazumi Shrine|en|Ōyamazumi Shrine|qid=Q703904|lt=Ōyamazumi Shrine|1=Ōyamazumi Shrine}}, located on '''Ōmishima Island in the Seto Inland Sea'''.  
In the past, it was said to rival its main shrine in grandeur.<ref>Ehime Prefecture Shrine Office</ref> The '''worship hall, built during the Sengoku period''', has been designated as an '''Ehime Prefecture Tangible Cultural Property'''.  
Following the '''Tenshō War Fires''' (天正の兵火), Bekku Ōyamazumi Shrine was managed by '''Nankōbō (南光坊)''', a temple that acted as its '''Bettō-ji (shrine-affiliated temple)'''. During the Edo period, pilgrimage records referred to it as:  
*"Japan’s Grand Protector deity (日本総鎮守) Ōyamazumi Daimyōjin, Bettō Nankōbō."*<ref>1825 pilgrimage record</ref>  
After the '''Meiji Restoration’s separation of Shinto and Buddhism (神仏分離)''', Nankōbō was formally separated, and the shrine’s '''pilgrimage site number was reassigned'''. However, even today, visiting both Bekku Ōyamazumi Shrine and '''Nankōbō''' remains customary.  
== Enshrined deity ==  
- '''Ōyamatsumi no Ōkami (大山積大神)''' – The deity of '''mountains and warriors'''  
- The shrine is an '''offshoot of Ōmishima’s Ōyamazumi Shrine''', but its '''name and deity’s representation differ from the main shrine.'''  
== History ==
[[File:Bekku20210511 1.jpg|thumb|Worship Hall/Main Hall]]
According to the shrine legend, in Taihō 3 (703 AD), Ochi Tamatsumi was ordered by Emperor Monmu to invite the deity from {{ill|Ōmishima Island|en|Ōmishima Island|qid=Q9009869|lt=Ōmishima Island|1=Ōmishima Island}} to Hiyoshigō, Ochi District, establishing it as the branch (Jigozen) of the main shrine, Ōyamazumi Shrine.
In Wadō 5 (712 AD), the shrine building was completed (some theories consider this as the founding date). The main shrine was initiated in Taihō 1 (701 AD) and its building was completed with the relocation ceremony held in Yōrō 3 (719 AD), so it may be said that the branch shrine is older. Thereafter, a branch family of the main shrine's priestly lineage served as the priests here.
During the Shōji era (1199–1200), eight of the twenty-four monk quarters of the main shrine were relocated from Ōmishima to the branch shrine and designated as subsidiary chapels of the separate temple, Daisekizan Kōmyō-ji. During the Kōnin era (810–824), when Kūkai visited and conducted religious rites in the quarters, it later became designated as one of the 88 pilgrimage sites of Shikoku. The Edo period pilgrimage record states "Japan's General Guardian Shrine, Mishima Main Shrine, Separate Temple Jingu-ji"<ref>1856 pilgrimage record</ref>.
In Tenbun 20 (1551 AD), the shrine building was consumed by fire due to a lightning strike, and it was rebuilt in Tenshō 3 (1575 AD). The eight monk quarters were burned down during the Tenshō era (1573–1592), and later only the Nankōbō was reconstructed, becoming the separate temple of this shrine.
In the early modern period, it was protected by successive lords of the {{ill|Imabari Domain|ja|今治藩主|lt=Imabari Domain|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imabari Domain|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} including Tōdō Takakage.
In the early Meiji period, due to the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, the Buddhist images and the pilgrimage designation were transferred to the Nankōbō, thereby dissolving the separate temple relationship.
In Showa 12, a new shrine building was constructed. At that time, the worship hall was relocated elsewhere and repurposed as an Ema hall.
In Showa 20 (1945), although most of Imabari City was destroyed by U.S. air raids—with only the main hall remaining—the former worship hall survived. During reconstruction, the former worship hall was returned to its original location and once again served as the worship hall.
== Cultural Properties ==  
=== Ehime Prefecture Designated Cultural Properties ===  
- '''Worship Hall (拝殿)''' – '''Built in 1575 CE,''' designated in '''1965 CE'''.  
- '''Rikai-ni’s Stone Lantern (理海尼の石灯籠)''' – Designated '''1984 CE'''.  
- '''Ema "White Horse" (絵馬「白馬の図」)''' – Designated '''1965 CE'''.  
=== Imabari City Natural Monuments ===  
- '''Camphor Tree (クスノキ)''' – Designated '''1974 CE'''.  
== Subordinate Shrines (Sessha and Massha) ==  
- '''Anaba Shrine (阿奈波神社)''' – Dedicated to '''Iwanaga-hime''', daughter of Ōyamatsumi.  
- '''Narabara Shrine (奈良原神社)''' – Enshrines a spirit relocated from '''Narabara Shrine in former Ochi District'''.  
- '''Kiyotaka Inari Shrine (清高稲荷神社)'''  
- '''Kōjin Shrine (荒神社)''' – Dedicated to '''Sanbō Kōjin''' and '''Ōkuninushi'''.

== Shrine Grounds ==
[[File:別宮大山祇神社 本殿.JPG|200px|thumb|Main Hall]]
* Main Hall
* Worship Hall – Rebuilt in Tenshō 3 (1575 AD). Designated as a tangible cultural property by Ehime Prefecture.
* Torii – The lintel bears the inscription "Japan's General Guardian Shrine, Mishima Jigozen."

== Major Festivals ==
* New Year's Festival (January 1)
* Ininen Festival (February 17)
* Hatsu-uma Festival (old date: First Horse Day in February)
* Annual Festival (Second Saturday)
* Wagoe (Natsu-goshi) Festival (July 29)
* Niiname-sai (Harvest Festival) (November 23)
* New Year's Eve Festival (December 31)
